quotes.text: If chapter 10 is indeed concerned with the conquest of Persia by Alexander the Great, as believed by most scholars, then chapter 11 foretells the division of Alexander's empire into two parts-the north headed by Seleucus and the south headed by Ptolemy.

This chapter is best understood as a prophecy of the end of the wicked world, the deliverance of the righteous with the help of Michael, the resurrection of the just and the unjust, and the assignment of "they that be wise" to their kingdom of glory. Thus far were these matters revealed to Daniel, but "knowledge shall be increased" more completely in "the time of the end" (Dan. 12:1-9 and fn.). Then, in conclusion to his many revelations, the prophet Daniel again saw angels beside the river and the same Being whom he had seen earlier and before whom he was overwhelmed-no doubt, the Lord (cf. Dan. 10:5-9). In Daniel's vision of the great events of the Resurrection, he perceived that some arise to undesirable status and some to everlasting life; they who are "purified and made white, and tried" may be those who will inherit celestial glory (Dan. 12:3, 10 and fn.; cf. Rev. 7:13-14). The book of Daniel has served to instruct many through the centuries because of its numerous teachings by example and precept. We may have to await future revelations to gain a full understanding of some of its more apocalyptic prophecies.
